content: The mathematical concept of a function describes a relationship between two quantities, where one quantity (the independent variable or input) determines the other (the dependent variable or output). A function assigns exactly one output to each input from a specified set, such as the real numbers. Functions can be represented in various ways, including through formulas, graphs, algorithms, or descriptions of their properties. In some cases, functions are defined in relation to other functions, such as inverse functions. In applied fields, functions are often specified using tables of values or formulas. It is important to distinguish between the function itself and the different ways it can be represented or visualized. A key concept in mathematics is the composition of functions. If one function depends on another, their composition creates a new function. For example, if ( z ) is a function of ( y ), and ( y ) is a function of ( x ), then ( z ) is a function of ( x ). This is achieved by using the output of the first function as the input for the second. This property of functions sets them apart from other mathematical constructs, such as numbers or geometric figures, and provides the foundation for the theory of functions. Functions are fundamental in all areas of mathematics, as well as in sciences and engineering. However, the understanding of functions, their notation, and even the meaning of the term function can vary across disciplines. In more abstract areas of mathematics, such as set theory, functions may not be defined by concrete rules or familiar principles. The essential property of a function, in its most abstract sense, is that it associates exactly one output with each permissible input. Functions need not involve numbers; for instance, a function might associate each word with its first letter or each triangle with its area. In algebra, functions are typically expressed using algebraic operations. In analysis, functions like the exponential function may have additional properties related to continuity, but they cannot always be defined by a single formula. In complex analysis, analytic functions are often defined concretely through their series expansions. In lambda calculus, a function is treated as a primitive concept rather than being defined in terms of set theory. Terms like transformation and mapping are often used synonymously with function, though they may have slightly different meanings depending on the context. Mathematical functions are frequently denoted by letters, with the standard notation for the output of a function ( f ) with input ( x ) being ( f(x) ). A function may be defined only for certain inputs, and the set of all acceptable inputs is called its domain. The set of all resulting outputs is called the range. In many fields, it is also important to specify the codomain of a function, which contains the range but is not necessarily equal to it. The distinction between range and codomain allows for questions of mathematical interest, such as whether the two are equal. For example, the expression ( f(x) = x^2 ) describes a function ( f ) of a variable ( x ), which could be an integer, a real or complex number, or even an element of a group. If ( x ) is specified as an integer, the function relates each input ( x ) to a single output ( x^2 ), obtained by squaring ( x ). Thus, the input ( 3 ) corresponds to the output ( 9 ), the input ( 1 ) to the output ( 1 ), and the input ( -2 ) to the output ( 4 ). This is written as ( f(3) = 9 ), ( f(1) = 1 ), and ( f(-2) = 4 ). Since every integer can be squared, the domain of this function consists of all integers, while its range is the set of perfect squares. If integers are chosen as the codomain, many numbers, such as ( 2 ), ( 3 ), and ( 6 ), are in the codomain but not in the range. In mathematics, functions are often introduced with temporary names like ( f ). For instance, we might define ( f(x) = 2x + 1 ), and then ( f(3) = 7 ). When a name for the function is unnecessary, the form ( y = x^2 ) is often used. If a function is used frequently, it may be given a more permanent name. The essential property of a function is that each input must have a unique output. For example, the formula ( y = pm sqrt{x} ) does not define a real function of a positive real variable because it assigns two outputs to each number. To make the square root a real function, we must specify which square root to choose, such as the positive square root. Functions do not always involve numbers. For example, a function might associate each word with its first letter or each triangle with its area. Functions are used in so many areas of mathematics and in so many different ways that no single definition of a function has been universally adopted. Some definitions are elementary, while others use technical language that may obscure the intuitive notion. Formal definitions are often set-theoretical and rely on the concept of a relation. Intuitively, a function assigns to each element of a given set (the domain or source) exactly one element of another set (the codomain or target). A simple intuitive definition for functions on numbers is that a function is given by an arithmetic expression describing how one number depends on another. For example, ( y = 5x 20x^3 + 16x^5 ) is a function where the value of ( y ) depends on the value of ( x ). This definition works well for elementary mathematics but is too restrictive for more advanced areas. For instance, the cosine function used in trigonometry cannot be written in this way; the best we can do is an infinite series. However, if we accept series as an extended sense of arithmetic expression, this definition served mathematics reasonably well for centuries. Eventually, the transformation of intuitive calculus into formal analysis required a broader definition. The emphasis shifted from how a function was presented—as a formula or rule—to a more abstract concept. Part of this new foundation was the use of sets, so functions were no longer restricted to numbers. Thus, we can say that a function ( f ) from a set ( X ) to a set ( Y ) associates to each element ( x ) in ( X ) an element ( y = f(x) ) in ( Y ). Note that ( X ) and ( Y ) need not be different sets; it is possible to have a function from a set to itself. Although the term associates in this definition can be interpreted with a concrete rule, it is essential to move beyond that restriction. For example, we can sometimes prove that a function with certain properties exists, yet not be able to give any explicit rule for the association. In fact, in some cases, it is impossible to give an explicit rule producing a specific ( y ) for each ( x ), even though such a function exists. In the context of functions defined on arbitrary sets, it is not even clear how the phrase explicit rule should be interpreted. As functions take on new roles and uses, the relationship of the function to the sets requires more precision. For example, in some parts of mathematics, including recursion theory and functional analysis, it is convenient to allow values of ( x ) with no association (in this case, the term partial function is often used). To discuss such distinctions, many authors split a function into three parts, each a set: ( f ) is an ordered triple of sets ( (F, X, Y) ), where ( F ) (the graph) is a set of ordered pairs ( (x, y) ), ( X ) (the source) contains all the first elements of ( F ), and ( Y ) (the target) contains all the second elements of ( F ).
